chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Said from Ibn Abi Umayr from Ahmad ibn Ishaq from Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him) who said:
I asked him: 'When a eunuch belongs to a man, he enters upon his wives and hands them the water for ablution, so he sees their hair.' He said, 'No (it is not permissible).'

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, who said: 'I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about the veiling of free women from the eunuchs.' He said, 'They used to enter upon the daughters of Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) and they did not veil themselves.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: 'This report (the second one) is considered to be from taqiyya (dissimulation), and the action is based on the first report. They only permitted it in the second report due to taqiyya from the ruler of the time.'

And it has been narrated in another hadith: that when he (peace be upon him) was asked about that, he withheld from answering and did not respond. And this indicates what we mentioned regarding taqiyya.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a eunuch seeing the hair of his master's wives?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* establishes the general prohibition of a eunuch (*khasi*) viewing the hair of a man's wives, a ruling derived from Imam al-Sadiq's direct negation. The subsequent report, noting that eunuchs did see the hair in the Imam's household, is interpreted by scholars like Muhammad ibn al-Hasan as an instance of *taqiyya* (dissimulation) to avoid political scrutiny from the ruling authority, thereby preserving the primary prohibition in practical jurisprudence. This distinction highlights the nuanced application of *taqiyya* in Shia fiqh to reconcile apparent contradictions between reported practice and legal ruling.
